hints: Focus on what both conditions mean together, a branched C5 skeleton plus an -OH on a carbon joined to two other carbons.
Start by listing the branched C5 skeletons, the 2-methylbutane skeleton and the 2,2-dimethylpropane skeleton, then test where -OH can go.
Try placing -OH to make it secondary on each branched skeleton and check for duplicates made by just renumbering from the other end.
walkthrough:
**Recall what secondary means**

Think of a secondary alcohol as C-OH where that carbon is attached to two other carbons and one H. So we need $\text{-CH(OH)-}$ in the middle of the chain, not at the end.

Rule:
$$\text{secondary alcohol carbon is bonded to 2 C atoms + 1 H + 1 OH}$$

**List the branched C5 skeletons**

For $\text{C}_5\text{H}_{12}\text{O}$ as an alcohol, the carbon backbone must have 5 carbons. There are only two branched options: the 2-methylbutane skeleton ($\text{C-C(C)-C-C}$) and the 2,2-dimethylpropane skeleton ($\text{C-C(C)(C)-C}$).

**Test the 2-methylbutane skeleton**

Put OH on carbon 2 of $\text{CH}_3\text{CH(CH}_3\text{)CH}_2\text{CH}_3$ to give $\text{CH}_3\text{CH(OH)CH(CH}_3\text{)CH}_3$, which is 3-methylbutan-2-ol. The C-OH carbon joins two carbons, so it is secondary and branched. This one counts.

**Test all other positions and the other skeleton**

OH on carbon 1 gives a primary alcohol, and OH on the branched carbon to give 2-methylbutan-2-ol gives a tertiary alcohol, so both fail. On the 2,2-dimethylpropane skeleton every outer carbon is primary and the central carbon has no H, so no secondary alcohol is possible. Also, 2-methylbutan-3-ol is just 3-methylbutan-2-ol renumbered, not a new isomer.

Conclusion: only 1 structural isomer fits.

options.A: Correct. Only 3-methylbutan-2-ol, $\text{(CH}_3\text{)}_2\text{CHCH(OH)CH}_3$, has both a branched skeleton and a secondary -OH carbon. All other branched placements are primary or tertiary or duplicates.
options.B: Too high. Students often count both 3-methylbutan-2-ol and 2-methylbutan-3-ol as different, but they are the same structure numbered from opposite ends.
options.C: Too high. Students often add in the straight-chain secondary alcohols pentan-2-ol and pentan-3-ol, forgetting the question requires a branched carbon skeleton.
options.D: Too high. Students often count every position of OH on the branched skeleton (1-ol, 2-ol) without checking primary versus secondary versus tertiary classification.
